name: AD4003BRMZ-RL7
title: AD4003: 18-bit, 2 MSPS differential SAR ADC, 1.8 V core, SPI, MSOP-10 and LFCSP-10
summary: An 18-bit successive-approximation converter with a fully differential input of ±VREF, sampling at up to 2 MSPS with no pipeline delay. The core runs from 1.8 V and the serial interface from a separate 1.71 V to 5.5 V logic rail; the reference (2.4 V to 5.1 V) is external. Features that ease driving it: high-Z mode lowers input current, span compression lets single-supply drivers stay off the rails, an internal clamp guards the inputs against overvoltage, and turbo mode allows 2 MSPS from a 75 MHz clock. It comes in a 10-lead MSOP and a 3 mm × 3 mm 10-lead LFCSP, specified from −40 °C to +125 °C.

circuits.title: Typical connection with split amplifier supplies
circuits.description: Two unity-gain op amps on a +6.5 V or higher and −0.5 V or lower rail each buffer one half of an antiphase signal that swings 0 V to VREF around VREF/2, and feed IN+ and IN− through an R-C low-pass. A reference, buffered by an op amp, gives 5 V at REF with 10 µF to ground; a 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider off that node gives the VREF/2 common mode. An LDO on V+ makes the 1.8 V VDD rail; VIO comes from the host's supply. The serial lines run straight to the host, 3-wire or 4-wire. The amplifier rails can be chosen for the widest signal range.

circuits.title: Single-ended to differential conversion with a fully differential amplifier
circuits.description: The fully differential amplifier turns a ground-referenced single-ended signal of ±VREF into the differential drive for IN+ and IN−. The signal enters through R3 (1 kΩ) on the +IN side, the R1 leg on the −IN side is returned to ground, and R4 and R2 (1 kΩ) close the two feedback loops. VOCM at VREF/2, decoupled with 0.1 µF, centres the outputs. The rest of the circuit matches the single-supply connection.

circuits.title: CS mode, 3-wire, no busy indicator
circuits.description: One converter on an SPI host. SDI is tied to VIO so every CNV rising edge selects CS mode; the host's convert line drives CNV, its clock drives SCK and SDO returns the data.

circuits.title: CS mode, 3-wire, with busy indicator
circuits.description: As the plain 3-wire hookup, with a 47 kΩ pull-up from SDO to VIO and SDO also wired to the host's interrupt input. The low-going edge on SDO at the end of a conversion tells the host to start reading.
notes: Supplies, reference and analog inputs connect as in the typical connections.

circuits.title: CS mode, 4-wire, two converters, no busy indicator
circuits.description: Two converters share the host's convert, clock and data-in lines. The host's CS2 line drives device A's SDI and CS1 drives device B's SDI, so both sample together and are read one after the other.
notes: Supplies, reference and analog inputs connect as in the typical connections.

circuits.title: CS mode, 4-wire, with busy indicator
circuits.description: CNV takes the host's convert line alone, so sampling stays independent of read-back; SDI is the chip select. A 47 kΩ pull-up from SDO to VIO and a link from SDO to the host interrupt give the end-of-conversion signal.
notes: Supplies, reference and analog inputs connect as in the typical connections.

circuits.title: Daisy-chain mode, two converters
circuits.description: Device A's SDI is grounded and its SDO feeds device B's SDI; B's SDO goes to the host. Both CNV pins share the convert line and both SCK pins the clock, so the pair shifts out 36 bits like one shift register, B's result first.

operation.text: A charge-redistribution SAR converter: two matched arrays of 18 binary-weighted capacitors sit on the inputs of a comparator. During acquisition the comparator side of each array is held at GND through SW+ and SW− while the other plates follow IN+ and IN−, so the arrays act as the sampling capacitors. When CNV rises, SW+ and SW− open, the arrays are switched off the inputs onto GND, and the control logic steps each capacitor between GND and VREF from the MSB down (steps of VREF/2, VREF/4 … VREF/262,144) until the comparator balances. The result and a busy signal follow. The conversion clock is internal; SCK plays no part in converting.

Up to 2 MSPS, with no pipeline delay: each result belongs to the sample just taken, which suits multiplexed inputs. The core powers down after each conversion, so power falls in proportion to sample rate (about 80 µW at 10 kSPS), and the first conversion after a long idle period is valid. 2 MSPS needs turbo mode and an SCK of at least 75 MHz.

Conversion takes 290 ns, and the input returns to tracking about 100 ns before the conversion ends, which lengthens the acquisition window. The longer window relaxes driver settling, permits a lower RC cutoff and a larger filter resistor with a smaller capacitor, and lowers dynamic power in the driver.

An internal clamp on IN+ and IN− turns on when an input rises 0.4 V above VREF, ahead of the ESD diode to REF, and sinks up to 50 mA to ground so the reference is not pulled up; this matters when several converters share one reference. With an external series resistor (REXT, 200 Ω up to 20 kΩ for 15 V protection) and a filter capacitor of at least 100 pF, no external protection diodes are needed. The clamp draws no static power while off but cannot hold an overvoltage forever. When active it clears the OV clamp flag (active low) in the register, a sticky bit cleared by reading it once the overvoltage is gone, and in the status bits, where it updates every conversion.

During acquisition each input looks like a pin capacitance CPIN in parallel with RIN (about 400 Ω, switch resistance plus series resistance) in series with CIN (about 40 pF, mostly the sampling capacitor). During conversion only CPIN remains. RIN and CIN form a single-pole low-pass that limits noise and aliasing.
The inputs sample the true difference IN+ − IN−, rejecting what is common to both. The two halves have to be exact antiphase (180°) so the common mode stays within VREF/2 ± 0.125 V.

Choose the RC filter and amplifier by signal bandwidth at full 2 MSPS (RC filter table); 200 Ω with 180 pF and the ADA4807-1 give the best general results. The large R and small C lighten the dynamic load and phase-margin burden on the amplifier and limit current into the input when the amplifier overdrives it. The driver's noise, filtered by the input RC or the internal RIN-CIN pole, has to stay small against the converter's 31.5 µV rms (driver SNR-loss equation); for ac work its THD has to match the converter's; for multiplexed use the driver and input must settle a full-scale step to 18-bit accuracy (3.84 ppm, 0.000384 %), which is much tighter than the 0.1 % to 0.01 % figures amplifier datasheets usually give. For single-ended sources the ADA4940-1 makes the differential drive. Performance holds up to Nyquist.

Set in the configuration register (off by default). It cuts the nonlinear kickback when the capacitor DAC switches back onto the inputs as acquisition begins, bringing input current down to the sub-microampere range for slow or dc signals and improving THD by about 10 dB up to 100 kHz, even with large source resistance. It costs about 2 mW per MSPS. Turn it off above 100 kHz input frequency and when multiplexing. With it, low-power precision amplifiers such as the ADA4077-1 (400 µA) and ADA4610-1 (1.5 mA) reach 96 dB to 99 dB SNR and better than −110 dB THD, and the filter resistor can be about ten times larger than on earlier SAR converters.

Set in the configuration register (off by default). Each input then only needs to swing from 10 % to 90 % of VREF (for example 0.41 V to 3.69 V with a 4.096 V reference) while all codes are still produced, which gives a single-supply driver its headroom and footroom. The differential full scale becomes ±0.8 × VREF and SNR drops by about 1.9 dB.

The REF input impedance changes dynamically. Bypass it with a 10 µF X7R ceramic in 0805 size. The ADR4550 gives best performance and drift; the ADR3450 saves power with slightly more noise. A buffer such as the ADA4807-1 between reference and REF is recommended, with the REF capacitance chosen both to keep the buffer stable and to meet the converter's own requirement.

Two supplies: VDD (core, 1.8 V) and VIO (logic, 1.8 V to 5.5 V). For 1.8 V logic VIO and VDD can share one rail. The ADP7118 LDO is suggested for VDD and VIO. No sequencing is needed between VIO and VDD, and the converter rejects supply ripple over a wide frequency range.

The SDI level at the CNV rising edge picks the mode: high selects CS mode, low selects daisy-chain mode. Because of the SDI hold time, tying SDI to CNV always gives daisy-chain mode. In CS mode the interface is 3-wire (CNV, SCK, SDO) or 4-wire (SDI, CNV, SCK, SDO, with CNV free of the read timing for low-jitter or simultaneous sampling). The busy indicator, a start bit ahead of the data that can interrupt the host, is enabled in CS mode when CNV or SDI is low at the end of a conversion; without it the host waits out the maximum conversion time. At power-up SDO is low or high-Z according to CNV and SDI (SDO power-up table).

Set in the configuration register; available in 3-wire and 4-wire CS modes and not in daisy-chain mode. It replaces the busy indicator and lets the previous result be read during the end of the current conversion, so a slower SCK suffices. It is required for 2 MSPS. In 4-wire turbo mode, wait tQUIET1 after CNV rises before pulling SDI low to read the previous result; leave tQUIET2 between the last SCK falling edge and the next CNV rising edge.

When enabled, six status bits (OV clamp flag, span compression, high-Z, turbo, two reserved) follow the 18 data bits. SDO goes high-Z after the sixth (not in daisy-chain mode), and the host need not clock them all before the next conversion.

One configuration register, written or read with a 16-bit frame while CNV is low: an 8-bit command (a 0, then seven command bits; leading 1s are ignored) followed by 8 bits of data. SDI is sampled on SCK rising edges and SDO changes on falling edges. A write needs SCK, CNV and SDI; to read the current result on SDO during a write, bring CNV low only after the conversion has finished, or the result may be wrong (the write still happens). Daisy-chain mode permits writes only, no reads. At the end of a transfer SDO goes high-Z on the CNV rising edge, or low if daisy-chain mode is on. Each register's LSB is reserved so that a 16-bit host can still set the final SDI level, which carries into the mode selection at the next CNV edge. For isolated systems the ADuM141D (75 MHz) supports 2 MSPS.

With SDI held high, a CNV rising edge starts a conversion, selects CS mode and puts SDO in high-Z; the conversion completes whatever CNV does afterwards. Without the busy indicator, CNV may go low during conversion to select other devices (a multiplexer, say) but has to return high within the minimum conversion time and stay high until the maximum has passed, then a CNV low puts the MSB on SDO. With the busy indicator, CNV goes back low within the minimum conversion time and stays low; SDO stays high-Z until the end of conversion, then drives low, which with a pull-up serves as an interrupt, and the data follow MSB first with an optional 19th clock. Data change on SCK falling edges and are valid on both edges; capturing on the falling edge allows a faster clock if the host's hold time allows. SDO returns to high-Z after the 18th (or 19th) falling edge, or earlier if CNV rises. Keep SCK quiet during conversion. Several busy-indicator converters selected together can contend on SDO without damage or latch-up.

With SDI high at the CNV rising edge, CNV starts the conversion and must stay high through conversion and read-back; SDI then acts as chip select. Without the busy indicator, SDI may select other devices early in the conversion but must be high again before the minimum conversion time and kept high through the maximum; afterwards, pulling each converter's SDI low in turn puts its MSB on SDO, so several converters share one data line. With the busy indicator, SDI goes low before the minimum conversion time and stays low; SDO drives low at the end of conversion as an interrupt with a pull-up. If SDI and CNV are both low, SDO is driven low.

SDO is held low while SDI and CNV are both low. A CNV rising edge with SCK low starts a conversion, selects daisy-chain mode and disables the busy indicator; CNV stays high through conversion and read-back. At the end of conversion the MSB appears on SDO and the remaining bits shift out on SCK falling edges while SDI shifts in the upstream converter's bits on rising edges, so N converters need 18 × N clocks and the maximum rate drops with the longer read-back. Registers can be written through the chain (4-wire, CNV low) but not read; status bits can be enabled to report each converter's configuration. Turbo mode is not available.

Keep analog and digital sections apart; the pinout puts analog pins on one side and digital on the other. Do not route digital lines under the part unless a ground plane beneath it shields them, keep CNV and clocks away from analog paths, and avoid analog-digital crossings. Use at least one ground plane, common or split; split planes join under the converter. Put the REF capacitor right against the REF and GND pins with wide, low-impedance traces, and place 100 nF ceramics for VDD and VIO close to the part with short, wide traces.
EVAL-AD4003FMCZ is the evaluation board, controlled from a PC through EVAL-SDP-CH1Z.

Output is 18-bit twos complement. 1 LSB is 38.15 µV with VREF = 5 V (30.5 µV with span compression). The first transition sits ½ LSB above −FSR and the last 1½ LSB below +FSR (−4.999981 V and +4.999943 V for the ±5 V range); zero error is measured at midscale and gain error from the first and last transitions.
Pin compatible with the 16-bit, 2 MSPS AD4000 and the other MSOP/LFCSP precision SAR converters in the family table.
